passage: I'm Gopika, and I run the second-hand book stall at our college gate with Arnab. I can only tell you what I've seen, not what's in his head. In June he bought forty copies of an old-syllabus exam guide cheap, sure they'd sell. They didn't. The syllabus had changed. Every week I say, "Let's sell them to the raddi shop and use the shelf." Every week he says, "Wait. Someone will need them. If we sell now, we've lost the money." They're still there, gathering dust, taking half our shelf. Meanwhile, when the new engineering drawing books started flying off the table, Arnab sold the last five at cost the same afternoon. "Take the profit before it disappears," he said. We ran out by Monday, and ten students came asking. I don't get it. The good ones he can't let go of fast enough.

qa.q: How many copies of the old-syllabus exam guide did Arnab buy?
qa.a: He bought forty copies.

qa.q: Why might Arnab keep the old guides even though they don't sell?
qa.a: Selling them to the raddi shop would make the loss real and final. Waiting lets him avoid that pain, so holding on feels like the safer choice.

qa.q: What could Arnab ask himself to decide about the old guides more clearly?
qa.a: He could ask whether he would buy forty of those guides today for the space they take. If not, selling them and using the shelf for books that sell is the better choice from here.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel about sharing a stall with Arnab's habits?
qa.a: Gopika seems frustrated and puzzled, watching dead stock take half the shelf while the popular books run out too early.

grounding: A stall partner describes a student who holds on to unsellable stock to avoid facing the loss, while selling the best-selling books too soon.

passage:
January. With her first internship stipend, Usha, twenty-one, bought small amounts of two companies' shares. Within a month, one had risen 8% and one had fallen 12%. She sold the rising one straight away. "Lock it in before it drops," she told her friend Vishal. The falling one she kept. "It'll come back. If I sell, I've lost."
April. The one she sold had gone up another 20%. The one she held had fallen further. Usha stopped opening the app. She felt sick every time she thought of it, so she didn't think of it.
July. Vishal asked, "If you had this money in cash today, would you buy that company?" Usha was quiet. "No." "Then why are you holding it?" "Because selling means admitting I lost." She said it out loud and it sounded strange even to her. That night she wrote down what she'd learned before doing anything else.

qa.q: How much had the falling share dropped within the first month?
qa.a: It had fallen 12%.

qa.q: Why did Usha stop opening the app in April?
qa.a: Looking at the falling share made her feel sick, and avoiding it let her escape the pain of facing the loss. Not looking felt easier than deciding.

qa.q: What question from Vishal was the turning point, and why?
qa.a: "If you had this money in cash today, would you buy that company?" It made Usha judge the share from today, not from what she paid, and she saw she was holding it only to avoid admitting the loss.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt watching Usha across these months?
qa.a: Vishal was probably worried but patient, waiting for the right moment to ask one clear question instead of lecturing.

grounding: A young woman sells a rising share too soon and holds a falling one to avoid facing the loss, until a friend's question makes her see it.

passage:
"So it's settled," said Papa. "Eshaan gets my study room for his exam year."
"No, no," Mummy said. "Where will you do your office calls? You'll lose your room."
Papa's face tightened. "I'm not losing anything. I'm fine."
But he wasn't. Chinmay, twenty-five, watched his father fold his arms. The room had been his for fifteen years.
"Papa," Chinmay said, "what if we put it differently? You keep the desk and the morning hours till nine. Nobody touches your bookshelf. Eshaan gets the room after school. And honestly, you do give up your evenings there. That's real."
Papa looked at him. "At least you're not pretending."
Eshaan chimed in, "I'll keep your shelf dusted, Papa."
Papa sighed. "Fine. Mornings are mine."
Later Mummy whispered to Chinmay, "How did you do that?"
"I just told him what he keeps, and what he loses."

qa.q: Until what time does Papa keep the desk?
qa.a: The morning hours till nine.

qa.q: What did Chinmay seem to notice when his father folded his arms?
qa.a: He seemed to see that Papa felt he was losing his room of fifteen years, and that the loss mattered more to him than the family's gain.

qa.q: Which way of framing the proposal helped Papa agree?
qa.a: Chinmay showed what Papa would keep, the desk, mornings and bookshelf, and honestly admitted what he'd give up, his evenings. That made the change feel fair.

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel when Papa finally agrees?
qa.a: Eshaan is likely relieved and grateful, and his offer to dust the shelf shows he wants Papa to feel respected, not pushed out.

grounding: In a family scene, a young man notices his father resisting losing his room and frames the plan around what he keeps while admitting what he gives up.

passage: I'm Gautam, the youngest man on the staff of a school in Indore, and in my second year teaching I watched a staff meeting go badly and then better. The principal wanted to replace our fixed Saturday half-day with two full Saturdays off each month. On paper, it was more rest. But the teachers exploded. "We'll lose our Saturday afternoons!" Jaya ma'am said. "Every week, gone." Nobody heard the gain at all. I noticed they fought to keep what they had much harder than they welcomed something equal or bigger. After the meeting I asked the principal if I could redraft the note. I wrote: "You keep: every Sunday, and two whole free Saturdays each month. You give up: the Saturday half-day on the other two weeks. That is a real loss, and we won't pretend it isn't." At the next meeting Jaya ma'am read it twice. "Well, at least it's honest." The vote passed.

qa.q: What did the principal want to replace?
qa.a: Our fixed Saturday half-day, with two full Saturdays off each month.

qa.q: Why did the teachers react so strongly to a change that gave them more rest?
qa.a: Losing something they already had, the weekly half-day, felt much bigger than gaining whole Saturdays. The loss grabbed their attention and the gain went unheard.

qa.q: What did Gautam change in the note, and why did it help?
qa.a: He listed what teachers keep and what they give up, and admitted the loss was real. Seeing both clearly, with honesty, made the change easier to accept.

qa.q: How might Jaya ma'am feel reading the new note?
qa.a: She seems to feel respected rather than tricked, since the note admits the loss, which is why she says "at least it's honest."

grounding: A young teacher notices colleagues fighting to keep a benefit, and redrafts the proposal to show what is protected and honestly admit what is lost.

passage: I'm Shalini, and I watched my cousin Lalremsiami make a decision in her little weaving room in Aizawl last month. A cooperative had offered to take her shawls: steady monthly orders, but they would set the prices. She'd always set her own. At first she said, "No way. I'll lose my freedom." That seemed to be the whole story for her. Then she did something I've never seen anyone do. She took a notebook and drew two columns. On one side she wrote what she'd lose: choosing prices, some special orders. On the other, what she'd gain: regular money, no chasing buyers. She tried to make them the same size. Then she asked herself aloud, "If I already had the steady orders, would I trade them for price freedom?" She thought for a long time. "No," she said. I don't know everything she felt, but she signed the next day.

qa.q: What did the cooperative offer Lalremsiami?
qa.a: Steady monthly orders, but they would set the prices.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami first say "No way"?
qa.a: Losing her freedom to set prices felt huge and immediate, so at first it drowned out the gain of steady orders.

qa.q: What question did Lalremsiami ask herself, and how did it help her decide?
qa.a: She asked, if she already had the steady orders, would she trade them for price freedom. Turning the gain into something she might lose made both sides weigh evenly, and she chose the orders.

qa.q: How might Shalini see Lalremsiami after watching this?
qa.a: Shalini seems impressed and curious, calling it something never seen before, and may try the two-column method too.

grounding: A cousin watches a young weaver weigh an equal loss and gain in two columns and ask which she would truly prefer, easing her pull toward the safe option.

passage:
Tuesday. Dilnaz got the offer: a job with a higher monthly salary but no year-end bonus. Her current job paid less each month but gave a bonus that made the total about the same. "I can't give up the bonus," she told her friend Zeenat at once. "What if the new place doesn't work out?"
Thursday. Zeenat came over with samosas. "Try this. Imagine you're already at the new job. Would you swap the higher monthly pay for a bonus that might come?" Dilnaz laughed. "When you say it like that, the bonus sounds risky." She took a sheet of paper and wrote both options in the same words: what she'd lose, what she'd gain, same size.
Saturday. She read the page again with fresh eyes. The totals really were about equal. What she actually wanted was the steadier monthly money for rent. She emailed the new company. "I accept."

qa.q: What did the new job not offer?
qa.a: No year-end bonus.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz first say "I can't give up the bonus"?
qa.a: Losing something she already had felt much bigger than gaining an equal amount, so the safe option of staying felt right without her really comparing.

qa.q: What did Zeenat suggest, and why did it change Dilnaz's view?
qa.a: Zeenat asked her to imagine already having the new job and whether she'd swap it for the bonus. Flipping which side counted as the loss let Dilnaz weigh both evenly.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel when Dilnaz accepts the new job?
qa.a: Zeenat is probably glad to have helped Dilnaz think clearly rather than pushing her either way.

grounding: A young woman imagines an equal loss and gain from both sides before deciding on a job, easing her automatic pull toward staying.

passage: In their Guwahati flat, Bhupen, five, clutched a small yellow rubber duck he'd won at the fair that morning. His cousin Alka held out her big shiny racing car. "Swap? Just for today?" Bhupen shook his head hard and hid the duck behind his back. "It's mine." Alka put the car down beside him. "You can have it to keep." He looked at the car. He looked at the duck. He pressed the duck to his cheek. "No. My duck." At bath time he took the duck into the bucket. The car stayed on the floor.

qa.q: Where had Bhupen won the yellow rubber duck?
qa.a: At the fair that morning.

qa.q: What does Bhupen pressing the duck to his cheek suggest he feels?
qa.a: It suggests the duck feels very special to him now that it is his, even more than a bigger, shinier car.

qa.q: How could Alka make a swap easier for Bhupen next time?
qa.a: She could let him play with the car while keeping his duck, instead of asking him to give up something that is his.

qa.q: How might Alka feel when Bhupen refuses even a keep-forever swap?
qa.a: Alka might be surprised or a little hurt, since she was offering her best car and he chose a small duck.

grounding: A young boy refuses to swap his new rubber duck for his cousin's bigger car, because the duck is his.

passage:
"Amandeep, look! Harleen's dinosaur roars!" said Chandrika Bua.
Amandeep, five, held his small green dinosaur from the cereal box. "Mine is better."
"Hers is bigger. It has a button. Want to swap?"
"No!"
"Just for a minute?"
"No. This is mine." He hugged it to his tummy.
Harleen pressed the button. ROAR. Amandeep's eyes went wide. He watched for a long time.
"Swap now?" Bua asked.
He shook his head. "Mine is the best one."
He put his green dinosaur on his pillow and patted it.

qa.q: Where did Amandeep's small green dinosaur come from?
qa.a: From the cereal box.

qa.q: What does Amandeep hugging the dinosaur to his tummy show about how he feels?
qa.a: It shows that the dinosaur feels precious to him because it is his, even though Harleen's is bigger and roars.

qa.q: What could Chandrika Bua try so that Amandeep can enjoy the roaring dinosaur?
qa.a: She could let him press the button while he keeps holding his own, so he doesn't have to give anything up.

qa.q: How might Harleen feel when Amandeep keeps saying his is better?
qa.a: Harleen might feel a bit puzzled or proud of her roaring dinosaur, and may not understand why he won't swap.

grounding: A five-year-old refuses to swap his small cereal-box dinosaur for his cousin's bigger roaring one, insisting his is best.

passage: Swati, you want to know why your Pappu Nana and I didn't talk for a week in 1966? Let your Neelam Dadi tell you. He was ten, I was eight, and he loved one cricket card: a bowler in mid-jump, with a torn corner. In our Meerut lane any card was worth two marbles, three at most. Pappu wanted ten. "It's worth more because it's mine," he said. None of the boys would pay. He came home furious. "They're all cheating me!" I said, "Bhaiya, would you give ten marbles for Bunty's card?" "Of course not, his is ordinary." I laughed, and he stopped talking to me. He never sold it. It's still in his tin box. He showed it to you last Diwali, remember?

qa.q: How many marbles did Pappu want for his card?
qa.a: Ten marbles.

qa.q: Why did Pappu think the other boys were cheating him?
qa.a: The card felt very special because it was his, so their offers of two or three marbles seemed unfair. He couldn't see that to them it was an ordinary card.

qa.q: What question did young Neelam ask, and how could it have helped Pappu?
qa.a: She asked if he would give ten marbles for Bunty's card. If he had thought about it, he might have seen that buyers and owners value the same thing very differently.

qa.q: How might the other boys in the lane have seen Pappu's price?
qa.a: They probably thought ten marbles was silly for a torn card and may have been annoyed at being called cheats.

grounding: A grandmother recalls her brother as a boy who demanded far more for his card because it was his, and thought the others were cheating.

passage: The school bus left in six minutes, and the card swap on the back benches was ending. Uday, eleven, held up his silver goalkeeper card. "Fifty rupees, or five cards." His classmate Harsha laughed. "Those are twenty. I'll give you twenty." "Twenty? It's mine. I've had it since Class 4." "It's the same card the stationery shop sells." The driver honked. Two more boys offered fifteen and twenty. "You're all cheating," Uday said, face hot. Harsha shrugged and got on the bus. Uday climbed on last, card in hand. Halfway home he thought: if it were Harsha's card, would I pay fifty? He didn't like the answer. He put the card in his pencil box and said nothing.

qa.q: How much did Harsha offer for the silver goalkeeper card?
qa.a: I'll give you twenty.

qa.q: Why did Uday feel the others were cheating him?
qa.a: He had owned the card since Class 4, so it felt worth much more to him. The buyers only saw an ordinary shop card, and he took their lower offers as unfair.

qa.q: What question did Uday ask himself on the bus, and how could it help him next time?
qa.a: Whether he would pay fifty if it were Harsha's card. Asking this before setting a price could help him see the gap between what owners and buyers think.

qa.q: How might Harsha see Uday calling everyone cheats?
qa.a: Harsha probably thinks it's a bit unfair and silly, since twenty is the normal price, and just shrugs it off rather than arguing.

grounding: A boy rushing for the bus demands far more for his card because it is his, and accuses buyers of cheating when they won't pay.

passage:
Monday. Sahil, twenty, had written the first draft of the college magazine's cover story: a long, dreamy piece about the canteen's history. Keerthana, the editor, read it and said, "Nice, but the students' strike about canteen prices is the real story. Could you rework it around that?" Sahil held the pages tight. "This one's mine. I wrote it at 2 a.m. It's good."
Wednesday. Keerthana showed him the new angle drafted by another writer, sharper and more urgent. Sahil read it and felt a small drop in his stomach. He still thought his draft was better, but he couldn't say why, except that it was his.
Friday. He sat with both pieces at the library. He asked himself: if both were written by strangers, which would I pick? The strike piece. Clearly. He walked to Keerthana's desk. "Use the strike angle. Maybe my history bit can be a side box." She grinned. "Deal."

qa.q: What was Sahil's first draft about?
qa.a: A long, dreamy piece about the canteen's history.

qa.q: Why did Sahil feel his draft was better even when he couldn't say why?
qa.a: Because he wrote it, at 2 a.m., it felt more valuable to him than any other version. His ownership made the draft seem better than it was.

qa.q: What question did Sahil ask himself on Friday, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Which piece he'd pick if strangers had written both. The honest answer, the strike piece, led him to suggest using it with his history as a side box.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have felt when Sahil walked up to her desk on Friday?
qa.a: Keerthana was probably relieved and pleased, having waited patiently for Sahil to see it himself.

grounding: A student clings to his own first draft over a clearly better angle until he asks which he would choose if strangers wrote both.

passage: Sonali, your chacha has a confession. When I was twenty, I had an old guitar with a cracked neck. I'd bought it second-hand at sixteen and learned every song on it. In my final year I needed a laptop, and I decided to sell the guitar. I put it up for eight thousand. The music shop offered two. A friend offered two and a half. I was outraged. "Do you know how many songs I've played on this?" I kept it listed for four months. Meanwhile I wrote my project reports in the cyber café, paying by the hour. One day my roommate asked, "Saurabh, if you saw this guitar in a shop for eight thousand, would you buy it?" I laughed. Of course not. The neck was cracked. That was the day I understood it was worth eight thousand only to me. I sold it the next week.

qa.q: How much did the music shop offer for the guitar?
qa.a: The music shop offered two.

qa.q: Why was Saurabh outraged by the offers?
qa.a: The guitar held years of songs and memories for him, so it felt worth far more than its market price. Owning it made it feel special.

qa.q: What question from the roommate was the turning point?
qa.a: "If you saw this guitar in a shop for eight thousand, would you buy it?" It made Saurabh see the guitar the way a buyer would.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel hearing that Saurabh chacha kept a cracked guitar listed for four months?
qa.a: Sonali might find it funny and touching, and it could help Sonali notice when something feels precious just because it is owned. 😊

grounding: An uncle tells Sonali how at twenty he refused to sell his old guitar at the market price because it was his.

passage:
Note in the flat's shared notebook. Written by Asif, Karthik's flatmate and team lead, Sunday.
Karthik put his three-year-old phone up for sale this week for twenty-two thousand. Buyers offered nine, ten, eleven at most. He was annoyed each time. "They don't get it. The camera's still good, and I've taken such care of it." I didn't argue about the price. Instead I asked him, "If you walked into a shop today and saw this exact phone, same scratches, same battery, would you pay twenty-two for it?" He opened his mouth to say yes, then stopped. "No. I'd pay maybe twelve." He looked a bit sheepish. What I did next: I showed him three similar listings, all under thirteen. He dropped his price to twelve that evening. I've noticed I do the same with my old bike, so this note is for me too.

qa.q: What price did Karthik first put on his phone?
qa.a: Twenty-two thousand.

qa.q: Why did Karthik feel buyers "don't get it"?
qa.a: Having taken care of the phone for three years, it felt worth more to him than to anyone else. He saw value in its history that buyers didn't.

qa.q: What question did Asif ask, and why did it work better than arguing?
qa.a: Whether Karthik would pay twenty-two for the same phone in a shop today. It let Karthik look at the price as a buyer and reach the answer himself.

qa.q: How might the buyers have felt when Karthik rejected their offers?
qa.a: They probably felt the price was unrealistic and moved on to cheaper listings.

grounding: A flatmate notes a seller pricing his used phone far above offers, and helps him check whether he would pay that price today.

passage:
Thursday night
Our flatmate Devesh has been trying to sell his old phone for two weeks. He's asking eighteen thousand. Kavitha and I looked it up: the same model, used, sells for around eight. Tonight a buyer came over, a college student with exact cash. She offered nine. Devesh looked offended. "Nine? It still has the original box!" The student left. Kavitha whispered to me, "He'd never pay eighteen for it himself." So after dinner I asked him, gently, "Devesh, if you were buying this today, what would you pay?" He was quiet for a long time, turning the phone over. "Honestly? Ten." Then he laughed at himself a little. "Why does it feel worth more when it's mine?" I didn't have an answer. He's relisting it at ten tomorrow. I wrote this down because I have a whole shelf of old stuff I think is priceless too.
Shalini

qa.q: How much did the college student offer for the phone?
qa.a: She offered nine.

qa.q: Why did Devesh look offended at an offer of nine?
qa.a: As the owner, he valued the phone far above what buyers pay, remembering its box and care. The student's fair offer felt like an insult to him.

qa.q: What question did Shalini ask, and how did it change Devesh's price?
qa.a: "If you were buying this today, what would you pay?" Answering as a buyer, Devesh said ten and decided to relist it at that price.

qa.q: How might the college student have felt when Devesh turned down nine?
qa.a: She may have felt confused or annoyed, having come with exact cash for a fair price, and simply left.

grounding: A flatmate's diary records a seller pricing his old phone far above offers, and a question about what he would pay today.

passage: Every Saturday in Durban, Sami, eight, went to the public library with his big sister Lindiwe, sat at the same corner table by the fish tank, and ate the same jam sandwich at noon. This week, things had moved. The fish tank was now near the windows, and a reading nook with beanbags filled the old corner. Sami froze in the doorway. "Where's my table?" "Look, beanbags!" Lindiwe said. "I want MY table." He sat stiffly at another desk, arms folded, not reading. At noon he refused a new sandwich from the café and ate his jam one. After a while, he crept over to the beanbags, just to look. He sat on one. "It's… okay," he said. Then, quieter, "It's actually squishy."

qa.q: Where had the fish tank been moved to?
qa.a: The fish tank was now near the windows.

qa.q: Why did Sami refuse to enjoy the new beanbags at first?
qa.a: His usual table and routine felt safe and known, so any change felt risky, even though the new nook was fine.

qa.q: What small step helped Sami try the change?
qa.a: He crept over to the beanbags just to look, and then sat on one. Trying a tiny piece of the change let him discover it was okay.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe feel when Sami says the beanbag is squishy?
qa.a: She is probably relieved and amused after his stubborn start, and glad he tried it on his own.

grounding: A boy insists on his usual library table and sandwich when things change, then slowly tries the new beanbags.

passage: At the school's summer camp, the dining hall had a new menu: dosa, poha, fruit, or aloo paratha. Manvir, nine, sat at his usual end of table three and asked for aloo paratha, like every day. His friend Rajni said, "Try the dosa, it's crispy." "No. Paratha." Camp teacher Jasleen ma'am noticed that Manvir also walked the long way to the pool, past the kitchen, though a new garden path was shorter. "Why that way?" she asked. He shrugged. "It's my way." On Friday, Rajni dared him to walk the garden path with her. He went slowly, looking around. Butterflies circled the hibiscus. "Hm," he said. "Same pool at the end." The next morning he tried half a dosa.

qa.q: Where was Manvir's usual seat?
qa.a: At the end of table three.

qa.q: Why did Manvir keep walking the long way to the pool?
qa.a: The usual way felt safe because he knew it, and trying the new path felt like a risk, even though it was shorter and fine.

qa.q: What helped Manvir try something new, and what could adults learn from it?
qa.a: Rajni's friendly dare to walk the garden path together. A small, shared first try made the change feel safe, which led him to taste half a dosa too.

qa.q: How might Rajni feel when Manvir tries half a dosa?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased, as her patient invitations finally helped her friend try something new.

grounding: At summer camp, a boy sticks to the same seat, breakfast and route until a friend helps him try a new path.

passage: In their small town near Rampur, everyone in Irfan's family had taken arts after Class 10: his father, the schoolteacher; his uncles; his sister Tanuja, now doing a B.A. Irfan, fifteen, spent his evenings at the electronics repair shop in the bazaar, fixing radios and fans. On the day the stream forms came, he ticked arts without thinking. "That's what we do," he said. Tanuja looked at the form, then at him. "Irfan, you fix phones for half the lane. You love circuits. Did you decide this, or did it just happen?" He shrugged. "Changing means talking to Abbu, and science is harder, and maybe I'll fail." "Maybe," Tanuja said. "Or maybe you'll love it. You haven't actually chosen anything yet." Their mother, Zeenat, called from the kitchen, "Talk to your Abbu tonight, beta. He'll listen." Irfan stared at the form for a long time. Then he picked up the eraser.

qa.q: Where did Irfan spend his evenings?
qa.a: At the electronics repair shop in the bazaar, fixing radios and fans.

qa.q: Why did Irfan tick arts without thinking?
qa.a: Everyone in the family had taken arts, so it felt like the natural path. Changing meant effort and risk, like talking to Abbu and a harder subject.

qa.q: What choice did Irfan make at the end, and what made it possible?
qa.a: He picked up the eraser to rethink the form. Tanuja's question, whether he decided or it just happened, and Zeenat's encouragement helped him see he hadn't chosen yet.

qa.q: How might Tanuja feel watching Irfan tick arts without a second thought?
qa.a: She is probably worried he is giving up something he loves, and she cares enough to question him gently.

grounding: A teenage boy in a small town ticks the family's usual stream without thinking, until his sister asks whether he actually decided.

passage: For two years, Ankita had taken the private bus from her town near Karnal to college: forty rupees each way, packed, forty-five minutes of loud film songs. In January a new state bus started on the same route, twenty rupees, half-empty, twenty-five minutes. Her friend Jyoti switched on day one. "Come with me tomorrow," Jyoti said. "No, I'm fine. I know the private bus conductor, I know where to stand. It's comfortable." But Ankita still arrived late and tired every day, and she'd told Jyoti twice that month she was short of money for photocopies. "Comfortable?" Jyoti said. "You complain every day." Ankita laughed. "I'm just used to it." She thought about it that night. Changing meant a new stop, a new timetable, a new conductor. That was all. The next morning she waited at the state bus stop, a little nervous, with Jyoti.

qa.q: How much did the new state bus cost?
qa.a: Twenty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Ankita say she was "fine" on the private bus?
qa.a: It was familiar, and changing felt like effort, a new stop and timetable, so she called her habit comfortable even though she complained daily.

qa.q: What helped Ankita finally switch buses?
qa.a: Thinking it through that night and seeing that changing only meant a new stop, timetable and conductor. Going with Jyoti made the first morning easier.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel waiting at the state bus stop with Ankita?
qa.a: Jyoti is probably pleased and a bit amused, having watched Ankita complain for weeks while calling it comfortable.

grounding: A young woman keeps taking a slower, costlier bus only because it's familiar, calling it comfortable, until she sees how small the change is.

passage: In Edinburgh, Freya had been paying for a meal-kit subscription since her first term. Every week a box arrived: three recipes, measured spices, a little card. She didn't much like the food, and it cost almost twice what she'd spend at the market. Alejandro, her flatmate, watched her leave half a box of vegetables to wilt again. "Why don't you cancel it?" "It's fine. It's easy," she said. "Is it? You never cook two of the three." Freya shrugged. "Cancelling means logging in, finding the page, answering their 'are you sure' questions. And then I'd have to plan meals." "So you're paying extra to avoid ten minutes." She opened her mouth to argue, then closed it. That evening she found the cancel page. It took seven minutes. On Saturday she and Alejandro walked to the market together, and she bought just what she wanted.

qa.q: How long did it take Freya to cancel the subscription?
qa.a: It took seven minutes.

qa.q: Why did Freya say the subscription was "fine" even though she didn't like it?
qa.a: Cancelling and planning meals felt like effort, so staying felt easier. She called it fine because change seemed like work, not because she was really happy.

qa.q: What turned Freya's thinking around, and what did she do next?
qa.a: Alejandro saying she was paying extra to avoid ten minutes. She found the cancel page that evening and went to the market on Saturday.

qa.q: How might Alejandro feel walking to the market with Freya?
qa.a: Alejandro might feel glad she made the change, and perhaps relieved to stop watching vegetables wilt in their shared fridge. 🙂

grounding: A young woman abroad keeps an overpriced meal-kit subscription only because cancelling feels like effort, until her flatmate points it out.
